War Crimes. Violations of the laws of war—acts perpetrated during armed conflict that breach internationally recognized conventions governing treatment of civilians, prisoners of war, and the disabled. Though organized warfare has ancient codes of conduct, formal codification emerged only after World War II through the Nuremberg Trials and the Geneva Conventions. War crimes remain contested in application. Some acts are universally condemned, while others are debated as inherent to warfare, strategic necessity, or cultural context.

The Hague Conventions of eighteen ninety-nine and nineteen oh-seven first attempted to codify laws of warfare in international law, prohibiting certain weapons and mandating humane treatment of the wounded and prisoners. World War II generated atrocities on an industrial scale—Nazi genocide, Japanese medical experiments, and Allied bombing of civilian centers raised the question of whether all wartime killing could be prosecuted.

The Nuremberg Trials from nineteen forty-five to nineteen forty-six established the principle that military orders do not excuse crimes against humanity. Commanders and officials could be held personally accountable for atrocities. The Geneva Conventions of nineteen forty-nine, revised since, created binding international standards for treatment of prisoners, the wounded, and civilians. Subsequent protocols in nineteen seventy-seven extended protection further.

Hiroshima and Nagasaki in nineteen forty-five killed approximately two hundred thousand civilians in atomic bombings. Debate persists whether strategic bombing of civilian populations constitutes a war crime or is defensible as hastening war's end. The Nanjing Massacre from nineteen thirty-seven to nineteen thirty-eight saw Japanese forces systematically rape, torture, and execute an estimated three hundred thousand Chinese civilians. Japanese denial of the scale and nature of atrocities remained contentious for decades.

The My Lai Massacre in nineteen sixty-eight saw U.S. troops murder between three hundred forty-seven and five hundred four Vietnamese civilians including children. It became the definitive modern example of prosecutable war crime. Only the commanding officer, William Calley, was initially convicted. Prosecution of war crimes remains politically contested. Powerful nations block investigation of their own conduct, while weaker nations face disproportionate scrutiny.
